newsitem.title: UK: BT braced for grilling by shareholders.
newsitem.headline: BT braced for grilling by shareholders.

text.p: British Telecommunications Plc is bracing itself for a grilling at its annual meeting on Wednesday by alarmed shareholders after an unexpected profit warning from its American merger partner MCI Communications Corp.
Concerns over MCI's forecast last week of higher-than-expected losses have shaken the planned $20 billion transatlantic merger and wiped over 2.0 billion pounds ($3.4 billion) off BT's value.
Some analysts say the concerns are overdone.

But others blame a lack of due diligence or a misunderstanding of the high-risk, high-cost nature of investing in local U.S. markets for BT's optimism that the merger would yield "tremendous growth prospects".
BT, which was hoping to finalise the biggest transatlantic merger in history this autumn, declines to comment on reports that it is looking for heads to roll at MCI after the surprise profit warning.
Newspapers say BT wants the managerial scalps of MCI's president Tim Price and the group's chief financial officer Douglas Maine.

BT says only that after Wednesday's meeting in the Scottish capital Edinburgh, it plans to send top executives to America for face-to-face talks with MCI to establish how fundamental MCI's problems are, whether forecast losses can be minimised and whether terms of the deal need to be re-negotiated.

Although BT declines to identify who will be flying to Washington, the Financial Times says finance director Robert Brace and chief executive Sir Peter Bonfield are taking personal charge of the review.

BT's chairman Sir Iain Vallance and his counterpart at MCI, Bert Roberts, will be in Scotland to field investor questions at what looks likely to be a stormy shareholder meeting. But few major institutions said they would attend the meeting, saying that they were relying on the press to keep them informed.

MCI, blaming the stalling tactics of local monopoly telecom operators in America and a lack of regulatory control, said last week it expected an additional $500 million losses this year over expectations and an extra $700 million-$1.0 billion in 1998.

But far from scaling back investments, MCI wants to spend an extra $400 million this year alone, be in 20 more cities than they would have been otherwise and is willing to incur hundreds of million of dollars more losses to go after local U.S. monopoly operators.
Some analysts say MCI's dramatic profit warning is partly a political move to put pressure on U.S. telecoms regulators to open up local markets more quickly.

Adrian Goodall, telecoms analyst at SBC Warburg, says MCI's higher than expected start up losses in the local U.S. market are a temporary phenomenon. But he says a question mark still hovers over whether there is any long-term impairment of earnings potential.
Goodall believes BT shareholders can take some comfort from the fact that BT seems to have been instrumental in identifying and publishing MCI's new forecasts.

"BT seems to be doing the right thing by looking at business strategy, the terms of the merger and management reporting," he said. "There is still a chance that BT shareholders will be insulated from the value impact if BT successfully re-negotiates the deal."

Brokers BZW says in order to maintain forecasts of zero earnings dilution on the MCI deal, BT would need to revise the terms to 4.1 Concert shares per MCI share from 5.4 plus $6.0 cash. This would imply an MCI share price of $34 from a previous $45.

Meanwhile, BT's shares, which were trading down 5.0 pence at 451-1/2, 1355 GMT, are likely to be supported by institutional "dividend junkies" which need the stock in order to qualify for a special dividend of 35 pence later this year, analysts say.

"Any potential price decline in BT, which would be caused by lower proforma earnings and increased dilution, is likely to be muted by the reality of needing to own shares to collect the special dividend," Salomon Brothers says. ($ = 0.592 British Pounds)
